actions.description: List every session in the fleet.
Show whether the Gateway starts at login, and the per-OS mechanism.
Start the Gateway when you log in (Windows Run key / macOS launch agent / Linux systemd --user).
Do not start the Gateway at login.
Show this session's id, name, machine, and repository.
Rename the current session using CC_SESSION_ID.
Rename a session selected by full id, id prefix, or exact name.

Open a new session. By default on the local Director; --machine <name> starts it on another computer, and --director <id-or-name> starts it on ONE named Director (a machine runs several, and only this says which).
List every Director this account is running, on every machine, with the id and name that 'session spawn --director' accepts. A machine appears once per named Director instance.
List the ACTIVE Missions on the Gateway - the named bodies of work sessions attach to. Add --all (or --state complete|removed) to include ones that have been ended.
Create a Mission record on the Gateway and print its id.
Attach a session that already exists to a Mission, moving it if it already had one. Add --with-children to bring everything that session controls.
Detach a session from its Mission, leaving it attached to nothing.
Rename a Mission. Its id does not change, so every attached session stays attached and its WHY is kept.
Mark a Mission as FINISHED. It leaves the default list and is kept as a record - this is the ending to use when the work is done.
Remove a Mission that should not exist - a duplicate, a mistake, an abandoned idea. NOT an outcome: use complete for finished work. Soft, so the record is kept and can be reopened.
Return a completed or removed Mission to active.
List the computers this account can search and start applications on. A computer appears once cc-launcher is running on it and has registered with the Gateway.
List the applications installed on another computer. Omit the query to list everything. The names it returns are what 'machine launch --app' accepts.

Find files by name across every drive on another computer. Use * and ? to match patterns; a query containing a directory separator is matched against the whole path. The search is bounded by a result count AND a time limit, and reports which one stopped it when it ends early - so check the truncation before treating the answer as complete.

Ask whether one computer can complete a Director restart, BEFORE draining it. Changes nothing: no command is sent, no connection opened and no signal raised. It answers with a verdict and the reason - and separately with whether that machine's launcher would refuse a restart while sessions are still live, which is not the same question. A drain that cannot end in a restart is a fleet-wide close with paperwork, so ask first.

ASK for a Director restart on one computer, in your own words. This restarts nothing: it creates a request the owner accepts once, after the Gateway has checked that the machine can actually be restarted (refused on the spot otherwise, naming why). While one request is pending for a machine a second is refused, and a request nobody accepts expires after thirty minutes. After the accept the Director drains itself, restarts and restores alone.

Bring a drained fleet back onto a Director (after a restart, the NEW one). The DIRECTOR starts every seat on its own credential, under the owner the seat had when it was captured - an owner restarted in the same drain comes back first and is named by its new id. You name no owner and cannot. Each seat that fails is reported on that seat and the rest carry on; a seat that came back is never started twice. This is the restore step of the director-restart skill.
Where one restart request stands, with the owner's or the Director's reason.

Start an application on another computer, by catalogue name (--app) or by absolute path (--path). A name that matches several applications is refused rather than guessed at, so nothing unintended starts on a machine nobody is sitting at.

Park a session so it stops asking for attention, for a set number of minutes. Defaults to THIS session. A session holding ITSELF is always mid-turn, so the hold is deferred automatically and lands when the turn ends - there is no separate verb for that, and the reply says 'pending' when it deferred. A hold ends when it is released, when the owner types or speaks into the session, when the timer expires, or when the session starts work nothing explains. Another agent's message does not end it.

Compact a session's context and send it NOTHING afterwards. Compaction SUMMARIZES the conversation, so the session keeps what it has learned - unlike clearing, which throws it away. This is the housekeeping verb: use it on a session whose context is filling up but which is still working fine. It frees room and leaves the session where it was. For a session that is STUCK, use session-compact-continue instead. Waits for the compaction to finish, so it can take a minute or two.

Compact a session's context and THEN type a prompt into it - the owner's rescue for a stuck session. The Gateway REFUSES this to every agent: only the owner types into a session. An agent compacts with session-compact and then queues a message with message-send.

End a session NOW and print what actually happened to it. Ends the agent process on the machine that owns the session and removes its row. Use session done instead when it is fine for the session to finish what it is doing first. A reason is REQUIRED and is recorded with the stop: any session may stop any other in the account, and the recorded reason is what makes that safe to allow. It does NOT touch files - uncommitted changes in the session's worktree are left exactly as they were, and the answer says where they are. Stopping something already stopped SUCCEEDS, and the answer says whether no process was running or nothing in the account carries that identifier at all.

Take a pending deletion back off a session - the cure for having flagged the wrong one. Defaults to THIS session. Needs no reason: a stop carries one because it is destructive, and this is the safe direction.
Release a hold, bringing a parked session back into the normal roster.

Queue a message for a session. You may message only the session that started you and the sessions you started; the Gateway refuses anyone else, and limits you to 6 messages an hour and 1 per recipient every 10 minutes. Nothing is typed into the recipient: it reads the full text from its inbox when it is free, so the answer is 'queued', never 'delivered'. Target 'all' queues one copy for each of your workers. Messages are rare - put what you would have said in your report instead. --reply-wanted (one session only) asks for a reply without waiting: it prints a correlation id, the reply arrives in your inbox, and if none arrives by the deadline (--reply-by minutes, 60 by default) a no-reply notice arrives instead.

Answer a message that asked for a reply. The id is the correlation id (or message id) 'message inbox' showed. The reply goes to whoever asked, whatever your relationship to it; only the session the question was sent to may answer, once. It is not held to the message limits, and a reply after the deadline still arrives.

Read THIS session's inbox: every unread message in full, each marked read by this call. Reading is the acknowledgement - a message stays open until its recipient runs this. A reply is shown with the question it answers, and a no-reply notice with the question that went unanswered. --all adds the newest 200 messages read in the last 24 hours, so a read whose answer was lost can be recovered - for 24 hours, and only by asking.
Windows only: check that a message to a throwaway worker is queued.
Display current CC Director settings.
Get a CC Director setting by dotted key.
Set a CC Director setting by dotted key.
List all available CC Director setting keys.
Show the local CC Director config file path.
List Gateway schedules.
Show one Gateway schedule in full.
Show run history for a Gateway schedule.
Create a Gateway schedule.
Fire a Gateway schedule immediately.
Enable a Gateway schedule.
Disable a Gateway schedule.
Delete a Gateway schedule.
Show the Gateway endpoint used by schedule commands.
List the fleet's Skills - central capabilities held on the Gateway, one line each.
Print a Skill's full instructions - run this when you are ABOUT TO USE it, and follow what it says.
Show one Skill's metadata without its body.
Show a Skill's version history.
Pull a Skill into a directory (skill.json + SKILL.md + its files at their own paths) for editing.
Push a directory as the Skill's DRAFT. No agent sees it until you publish.
Publish a Skill's draft - live for every agent on every machine, immediately.
Clone a Skill into one of your own - how a read-only built-in is customized.
Make a Skill available again - back in every agent's briefing.
Switch a Skill off - left out of every briefing, fetch refused, nothing deleted.
List the fleet's Workflows (cross-agent conduct stored on the Gateway).
Print a Workflow's raw instruction markdown - fetch this and FOLLOW it as your conduct.
Show one Workflow's metadata, steps, and outcome criteria.
Show a Workflow's version history.
Pull a Workflow into a directory (workflow.json + instructions.md + helpers/) for editing.
Push an edited Workflow directory to the Gateway as a draft (creates the Workflow if new).
Publish a Workflow's draft - it becomes the version every machine and agent reads.
Write a Workflow's instructions and helper files to this machine's cache and print the paths.
List workflow runs (one row per execution; the governance outcome spine).
Show one workflow run: pinned version, lifecycle, acceptance, criteria, participants.
Turn a Workflow back ON (returns to agents' briefings; runs and seats resume).
Turn a Workflow OFF - hidden from agents' briefings, no new runs or seats; nothing deleted.
Clone a Workflow's published content into a new editable Workflow you own (the way to customize a built-in).
Archive a custom Workflow (built-ins can never be deleted; history remains).
Email the account owner (single recipient); optional file attachments. The escalation channel for unattended runs.
Show local DevThrottle setup status.
Install or repair DevThrottle from the latest GitHub release.
Update DevThrottle through the setup engine.
Repair DevThrottle through the setup engine.
Show local DevThrottle setup diagnostics and repair guidance.
Show which session this account has marked as its one Fleet Manager, or none.
Mark a session as this account's one Fleet Manager, replacing any earlier mark. With no session, marks the session running the command.
Remove this account's Fleet Manager mark.
List this machine's drivable browser profiles (name, browser, status, account).
Register a new drivable browser profile (does not launch it).
Open the account page for a one-time human sign-in; add --done to mark it complete.
Launch a profile if it is down, then print how to attach the harness.
Print the BU_NAME/BU_CDP_URL export lines to attach browser-harness to a profile.
Close a running browser profile cleanly (its login is kept).
